summary: Presents a list of Internet protocols and where each stood in the standardization process, with an explanation of the process and the terms used. It was reissued periodically as the status of protocols changed. It is now historic and was replaced by RFC 2300.

eli5.summary: It is a report card listing every Internet rule and how far along each one is in becoming official. A newer report card replaced it.

questions: what was the internet official protocol standards list
how did rfc standardization stages work in 1997
how do protocols become internet standards
what are draft standards and proposed standards
subtitle: How Internet protocols move through stages to become standards.

tldr.problem: The Internet community needs a shared understanding of which protocols are official standards, which are experimental, and what stage each protocol occupies in the standardization process.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2200 categorizes every protocol by two dimensions: its maturity level (Standard, Draft Standard, Proposed Standard, Experimental, Informational, or Historic) and its requirement level (Required, Recommended, Elective, Limited Use, Not Recommended), providing a matrix that shows the status of the entire protocol suite.
tldr.outcome: This document became the official reference for Internet standardization status, updated periodically to reflect protocol evolution. It is now historic, replaced by RFC 2300 and subsequent protocol status documents.

today: RFC 2200 is Historic. RFC 2300 replaced it, and the current Internet protocol status is maintained in updated status documents.

sections.title: Introduction and Purpose
sections.content:
RFC 2200 is the Internet Official Protocol Standards document, published by the Internet Architecture Board (IAB) to describe the standardization state of all protocols used in the Internet. It serves as the authoritative reference for understanding which protocols are official standards, which are still being tested, and which are obsolete.

The document explains the standardization process, defines terminology, and then lists hundreds of Internet protocols, grouping them by their current status. The IAB issued this document approximately quarterly to keep the Internet community informed as protocols advanced or were superseded.
sections.eli5: This document is like a report on all Internet rules. It tells you which rules are official, which are being tested, and which are old.

sections.title: The Standardization Process
sections.content:
Internet protocols follow a rigorous advancement path controlled by the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG) of the IETF. A protocol begins with a proposal and may advance through stages involving increasing amounts of scrutiny, testing, and implementation experience.

The path is strict: a proposed standard must wait a minimum of 6 months before advancing to draft standard status, and another 4 months minimum before becoming an official standard. At each step, the IESG must make an explicit recommendation. The process requires at least two independent implementations before a protocol can advance to draft standard, and operational experience with two or more interoperable implementations before reaching full standard.

The RFC series is the primary vehicle for all standards documentation. While anyone can submit an RFC, standards-track RFCs require IESG approval before publication. Once published, an RFC is never revised; instead, new RFCs document updated versions of a protocol.
sections.eli5: Before a rule becomes official, it has to be tested thoroughly. Everyone must agree on it, and it must work in real systems. This takes time to make sure the rule is actually good.

sections.title: Maturity Levels and Requirement Levels
sections.content:
RFC 2200 defines six maturity levels that describe a protocol's standardization state. A Standard Protocol is official, assigned an STD number, and divided into IP protocols (applying to the whole Internet) and network-specific protocols. Draft Standard protocols are actively being considered for standardization and need substantial testing. Proposed Standard protocols are candidates that may be standardized in the future, with revision likely. Experimental protocols are research work not yet intended for operational use. Informational protocols are from other standards bodies or vendors and published for community convenience. Historic protocols have been superseded or lack interest.

Separately, every protocol receives a requirement level describing its role. Required protocols must be implemented in all systems. Recommended protocols should be implemented. Elective protocols are optional. Limited Use protocols are for specific circumstances. Not Recommended protocols are discouraged. These two dimensions—maturity and requirement—form a matrix showing the shape of the protocol suite.
sections.eli5: Every protocol gets two labels. One says how done it is: brand new, being tested, official, experimental, or old. The other says whether you should use it: everyone must, everyone should, optional, or don't use.

sections.title: The Standards Track Diagram
sections.content:
The document illustrates the flow of protocols through standardization as a state diagram. A protocol enters the track as a proposed standard (typically after IESG recommendation), a temporary state lasting at least 6 months. From there it may advance to draft standard, another temporary state lasting at least 4 months. Draft standard may advance to the long-term state of standard. At any point, a protocol can be assigned to experimental or historic status.

Protocols in temporary states are expected to stay there for months while the community gains experience. Long-term states (standard and historic) may persist for years. Only IESG action moves a protocol along the track; without explicit IESG recommendation, advancement cannot happen.

The RFC Editor uses a decision table to determine how to process submissions based on source and desired status. Only IESG submissions are published as Standard or Draft Standard. Proposed standard submissions from the IESG are published, but from other sources are referred for working group review.
sections.eli5: Protocols climb a ladder. First they are proposed and tested for 6 months. Then draft for 4 months. Then official. Or they might be labeled experimental or old instead. Experts vote to move them up.

references.text: Postel, J., "RFC-1602: Internet Standards Process", October 1994.
